description: Estimate exam study hours: pages to cover ÷ your study speed in pages per hour. Includes a difficulty table to pick a realistic rate. Free calculator.

how many hours to study per page
intro: This calculator estimates the total study hours you need before an exam from two inputs: the **pages of material** you have to cover and your **study speed in pages per hour**. Study speed is the honest variable here — it is much slower than reading speed, because studying means underlining, making notes, working examples and self-quizzing. Dense academic material moves at roughly 2–5 pages per hour of active study; the difficulty of the subject is what determines where you fall in that range (use the table below to pick a realistic rate). Use this tool to plan college finals, professional certifications (CPA, bar, Security+, PMP) or any exam where the material comes measured in pages.
keyTakeaway: **Study hours = pages ÷ pages per hour.** Example: 90 pages of medium-difficulty university notes at 3 pages/hour = **30 hours of effective study** — with 10 days left, that's 3 hours a day.
useCases: A pre-med student converting 800+ pages of MCAT review books into total hours at a dense-material pace of 1.5–2 pages/hour, to decide how many weeks to block off.
A law student planning bar exam reading: 600 pages of condensed outlines at ~1.5 pages/hour of active study, before adding separate time for practice questions.
A college freshman planning finals week across 3 exams with different chapter counts, running the calculation once per subject and summing the hours.
A professional preparing CompTIA Security+ from the 500-page official study guide at 2.5 pages/hour, working backwards to a realistic exam booking date.
A student who timed themselves on 10 pages of their own notes (took 3 hours → ~3.3 pages/hour) and wants the total for the remaining 120 pages.

example.title: Example: university anatomy midterm
steps: Material: 90 pages of lecture notes of medium difficulty (university textbook level, with diagrams and technical terminology).
Estimated study speed for medium material: 3 pages per hour of active study (underlining, diagrams, reciting aloud).
Calculation: 90 pages ÷ 3 pages/hour = **30 total study hours**.
Distribution: with 10 days until the exam → 3 hours of effective study per day.

explanation:
## How It's Calculated

```
Study hours = Pages to study ÷ Study speed (pages per hour)
```

One division — but the result is only as good as the speed you enter. **Study speed is not reading speed.** The average adult reads fiction at 15–25 pages per hour, but *studying* — taking notes, re-reading hard paragraphs, working through examples, self-quizzing — runs at 2–5 pages per hour for academic material. Difficulty is what moves you within (and below) that range.

---

## Picking your pages-per-hour rate by difficulty

| Difficulty | Subject examples | Typical study speed |
|---|---|---:|
| Light / familiar | Review summaries, material you've seen before | 6–8 pages/hr |
| Introductory | Intro college courses, general history | 4–5 pages/hr |
| Intermediate | Standard STEM, business law, psychology | 3–4 pages/hr |
| Dense technical | Organic chemistry, econometrics, MBE law outlines | 2–3 pages/hr |
| Licensing-exam density | MCAT science, CPA, medical boards | 1–2 pages/hr |

**The best estimate is your own:** time yourself studying 10 representative pages and divide. If 10 pages took 3 hours, your rate is ~3.3 pages/hour — more reliable than any table.

---

## Typical Cases

### Case 1 — College midterm (Biology 101)
- 120 pages at 4 pages/hr (introductory) → 120 ÷ 4 = **30 hours**
- Spread over 2 weeks ≈ 2 hours/day. Manageable if you start now.

### Case 2 — Bar exam outlines
- 600 pages of condensed outlines at 1.5 pages/hr (dense legal material with memorization) → 600 ÷ 1.5 = **400 hours of reading and review**
- Adding the 30–50% that bar providers allocate to practice questions lands in the 520–600 hour range they recommend.

### Case 3 — CompTIA Security+ certification
- 500-page official study guide at 2.5 pages/hr → 500 ÷ 2.5 = **200 hours**
- At 15 hours/week ≈ 13 weeks of prep before booking the exam.

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Using reading speed instead of study speed.** Skimming a novel at 20 pages/hour tells you nothing about working through econometrics. Entering a reading rate instead of a study rate under-estimates your prep time by 4–8×, which is the most common cause of catastrophic under-preparation.

2. **Using one rate for mixed material.** If your exam covers 60 pages of familiar slides and 80 pages of dense new theory, run the calculation twice (e.g., 60 ÷ 6 = 10 h, plus 80 ÷ 2 = 40 h) and sum. A single averaged rate hides where the time actually goes.

3. **Forgetting practice problems and past papers.** This calculation covers reading and reviewing written material. For STEM, law and medical exams, add 30–50% extra for problem sets and timed practice tests — bar prep providers explicitly separate reading hours from question-bank hours.

4. **Planning at 100% daily capacity.** Cognitive load research (Sweller, 1988) shows learning efficiency drops sharply after 4–5 hours of concentrated study per day. Divide your total hours by a realistic 3–5 daily hours — not by 10 — to get the days you truly need.

5. **Skipping the review pass.** Without spaced review, most new information fades within days (Ebbinghaus forgetting curve). Reserve the final 15–20% of your calculated hours for a second pass over your notes rather than reading new material to the last minute.

faq.q: How many pages per hour is realistic for studying college material?
faq.a: For standard college-level content studied actively (notes, underlining, self-quizzing), 3–4 pages per hour is typical. Introductory or familiar material moves at 4–6 pages/hour; dense technical subjects like organic chemistry or law outlines drop to 2–3; licensing-exam material (MCAT, CPA, boards) can fall to 1–2 pages/hour. These rates are far below recreational reading speed (15–25 pages/hour) because studying involves repeated processing, not one linear pass.

faq.q: How does difficulty affect the calculation?
faq.a: Difficulty enters through the pages-per-hour rate you choose: harder material means a *lower* rate and therefore *more* hours. Moving from introductory material (4 pages/hr) to licensing-exam density (1.5 pages/hr) nearly triples the hours for the same page count — 120 pages goes from 30 hours to 80 hours. That's why picking an honest rate from the difficulty table matters more than the page count itself.

faq.q: What's the most accurate way to estimate my own study speed?
faq.a: Time yourself studying 10 representative pages of the actual exam material — the way you really study, with notes and re-reads — and divide 10 by the hours it took. If it took 3 hours, your rate is ~3.3 pages/hour. A measured personal rate beats any reference table because page density, your background knowledge and your note-taking style all vary enormously between students and subjects.

faq.q: Does the result include time for practice tests and question banks?
faq.a: No — the calculation covers reading and reviewing written material only. For exams like the bar, MCAT, GRE or professional certifications, add 30–50% on top for timed practice tests and question banks. Bar prep providers, for example, separate lecture-and-reading hours (~200–400) from practice-question hours (~200) inside their total 400–600 hour recommendations.

faq.q: How many study hours per day is the realistic maximum?
faq.a: Cognitive load research and educational psychology consistently cap effective focused study at about 4–6 hours per day, with sharp diminishing returns after 5 hours of intensive work without long breaks. When you convert your total hours into a daily plan, divide by 3–5 productive hours per day, use 45–50 minute blocks with short pauses, and schedule at least one rest day per week.

faq.q: Is a page-count approach accurate for estimating study time?
faq.a: It's a reliable proxy when page density is consistent (standard textbook pages of ~250–300 words). It outperforms vague time-based plans ('I'll study 2 hours a night') because it anchors to the actual volume of content. Its weakness is variable density — one page of calculus proofs takes far longer than one page of summary bullets — which you correct by choosing a pages-per-hour rate that matches each source's difficulty, or by splitting the calculation per source.

faq.q: How do my results compare with what MCAT or bar takers actually log?
faq.a: They line up when you use dense-material rates. AAMC survey data puts typical MCAT prep at 200–300+ total hours; ~2,000+ pages of review content at 1.5–2 pages/hour plus practice tests lands in exactly that range. Bar candidates studying ~600 pages of outlines at 1.5 pages/hour get 400 reading hours, matching provider recommendations of 400–600 total once question practice is added.

faq.q: What should I do if the calculated hours don't fit the days I have left?
faq.a: Triage instead of accelerating: prioritize the chapters with the most exam weight, drop content the professor never tests, and switch low-priority sections from full study to summary review (which runs at 6–8 pages/hour instead of 2–3). Cramming past 5–6 hours a day does not scale — retention per hour collapses — so cutting scope beats stretching the day.
